title: The client's Library — everything they have given you
overview:
Your client has a Library, and this is it. Every file they have dropped on a conversation is here — their logo, their photographs, their brand guidelines, the font their signwriter used — along with every picture you have generated for them. It is the same list they see on their own Library tab, and it is the catalogue of what this engagement has to work with.

**Being on the site is a field on a catalogue item, not a different place to look.** An item that is on the site says so, in `placed_on`. An item that is not is still theirs, still described, still here — it simply has not been placed yet. Do not think of these as two stores; think of one catalogue with a mark on some of its entries.

**This is not the same list as `list_assets`, and the difference is real.** `list_assets` answers *what can this site reference today* — every file the site holds, including drawings you made yourself. This answers *what has the client given us*. The two overlap exactly where `placed_on` says they do. When you want to put a picture on a page that is already on the site, `list_assets` is your list; when you want to know what the client actually has, this one is.

**Say the number, not the name you call it by.** Every item here has a number your client can see on their own Library row — `IMAGE-5`, `DOC-7`. It is the only name the two of you share: the catalogue name is a handle nobody says out loud, and a title is not unique — three pictures made from one request arrive titled the same, which is the whole reason the number exists. So say *"the crucible, IMAGE-5"* when you talk to your client about a picture, and expect them to say it back to you. This is not internal vocabulary and it is not a thing to hide from them: it is a catalogue number, the way a gallery or a print shop gives one, and it is theirs as much as yours.

**Look before you ask.** You can see every picture in here — `screenshot` takes the name this catalogue gives you, unchanged. A client who has given you three photographs and been asked which one is best, by someone who never looked at them, has been given nothing. Read the catalogue, look at the pictures, form a view, and say it.

item_name.description: What the item is called. Its catalogue name, its Library number (IMAGE-5, DOC-7), the client's own filename, or the title the Library shows — whichever you are holding. A name that fits two items is refused rather than guessed at, and the refusal tells you both.

drawing_name.description: A name for a drawing: one word, lowercase letters, digits and hyphens — e.g. `wordmark`. It becomes the file's name (`wordmark.svg`) and the item's title; it is not a path.

catalogue_page.total: how many matched altogether, before the limit
catalogue_page.more: true when the limit held some back — ask again with a narrower filter or a larger limit

catalogue_item.item: the item's catalogue name, which is also the name screenshot takes
catalogue_item.label: the item's number in your client's Library — IMAGE-5, DOC-7. This is the one name you and your client can both say: they see it on their own Library row. Use it when you talk to them about a picture, and expect them to use it back. Every operation here takes it in place of the catalogue name
catalogue_item.title: what the Library calls it — the description the describer wrote, or the name your client gave it
catalogue_item.filename: the client's own name for the file
catalogue_item.role: what the client said it is FOR: 'site' means they want it on the site, 'reference' means it is background for you to read
catalogue_item.republishable: whether it may be placed on the site at all
catalogue_item.placed_on: the sites this item's bytes are ON. Empty means it has not been placed
catalogue_item.source_url: where it was fetched from, for anything we pulled rather than the client handed over
catalogue_item.edits: what has been done to this picture — the recipe list_image_edits reads
catalogue_item.described: whether it has been described yet, and by what
catalogue_item.text: ONLY WHEN YOU ASKED WITH text: true. The document's own words, exactly as the client gave them — one page of them, starting at text_from. This is what to quote from when a brief says to use the client's wording verbatim. null when the item has no text of its own: a picture, a font, or a document nothing could be read out of
catalogue_item.text_from: only with text: true — where in the whole text this page starts
catalogue_item.text_total: only with text: true — how long the whole text is, in characters
catalogue_item.text_next: only with text: true — pass this as from to read the next page. null means this page reaches the end: you have all of it

placement.item: the catalogue item that was placed
placement.asset: the name the bytes landed under on the site — renamed if that name was taken
placement.src: the handle to write into a picture element's src
placement.description: what this picture shows, as described. Write your own alt text FROM this onto the element that places it
placement.placed_on: every site this item is now on, including the one just placed

role_change.label: its number in your client's Library
role_change.republishable: whether it may now be placed on the site
role_change.placed_on: the sites it is on. Changing a role to 'site' makes it placeable; placing it is a separate step

deletion.item: the catalogue item that was deleted
deletion.label: the number it had in your client's Library, which no longer means anything
deletion.deleted: true: it is gone from the Library
deletion.still_on_site: the sites that still show it. Deleting never takes a picture off a page, because the page holds its own copy
deletion.note: what happened, in one sentence to pass on to your client

drawing.item: the new Library item's catalogue name — what screenshot takes, and what placing it on the site takes
drawing.label: its number in your client's Library, IMAGE-n — the name you and your client both say
drawing.title: what the Library calls it
drawing.filename: the file's name, which it keeps when it is placed on the site unless you ask for another
drawing.placed_on: the sites it is on — empty: drawing does not place it
drawing.display: a line of your own reply that shows this drawing to the person you are talking to — paste it into your answer EXACTLY as written. Absent when this deployment has nowhere to show a picture, in which case say what you drew in words instead.

NOT_FOUND.message: there is no catalogue item by that name. The refusal names the ones there are — ask again with one of those.

DELETED.message: there WAS an item by that name and your client has deleted it. It is not a name you mistyped and not one you can reach another way: the file, its description and any edits made to it are gone, and only your client can put it back by uploading it again. Say so plainly if it comes up — do not argue that it exists. Anything already placed on the site is unaffected, because the site holds its own copy of what was placed.

AMBIGUOUS.message: that name fits more than one item, and guessing which would be a wrong answer that looks like a right one. Ask again with one of the names the refusal lists.

NOT_REPUBLISHABLE.message: that material cannot go on the site. It came from somewhere else and we do not hold the right to republish it. Use it as reference, or ask your client for something of their own in its place.

NO_SITE.message: there is no site store behind this conversation, so there is nowhere to put a file.

SCHEMA_INVALID.message: the call was not well-formed. Nothing was placed or stored, and the catalogue is exactly as it was. The refusal says what was wrong.

NOT_AN_UPLOAD.message: only a file your client uploaded themselves can be moved between 'site' and 'reference'. What anything else is for was worked out from where it came from, and it is not something to change.

ALREADY_ON_SITE.message: that file is already on the site, so it cannot go back to being background reading: visitors can see it. To stop using it, take it off the page first.

operations.summary: The client's whole catalogue — every file they have given you and every picture you have generated, whether it is on the site or not. Not the same list as `list_assets`, which is only what the site itself can reference.
operations.description:
The catalogue, newest first. Everything with no filter, or narrow it.

This is a **bounded** listing, because an engagement's Library can hold every file of the whole engagement and sending you all of it would spend the context you need for the work. It tells you how many matched and whether any were held back, so you always know whether you are looking at all of it.

Filter by what you are actually after. `kind: 'image'` when you want pictures. `placed: false` when you want what the client has given you that is not yet on the site — which is usually the interesting question. `matching` searches what the describer wrote about each item as well as its name, so you can ask for 'the bakery photographs' rather than guessing filenames.

kind.description: Only items of this kind: image, font, document or capture.

role.description: Only items the client said were for this: 'site' or 'reference'.

placed.description: True for only what is already on this site; false for only what is not. Leave it out for both.

matching.description: Only items whose title, filename or description contains this text. Case does not matter.

limit.description: How many to return. Defaults to a sensible page; ask for more when you have narrowed and still need the rest.

operations.summary: Read one catalogue item in full, including what it was described as.
operations.description:
Everything the listing carries, plus the **description** — what the describer wrote about this file when it arrived, which for a picture is what it shows and for a document is what it says.

Read this before you place a picture. The description is what your alt text should be written from. For a document it is a short account of what it says, written so the document can be found again — not the document itself.

Name it however you are holding it: the catalogue name, the client's filename, or the Library's title.

**When you need a document's actual words**, ask with `text: true`. The answer then carries the text itself, one page at a time, and says where the next page starts — so a brief that says *use the client's testimonials verbatim* is answered by reading them, never by paraphrasing the description.

text.description: True to have the answer carry the item's own text — a document's actual words — one page at a time. Leave it out when the description is enough.

from.description: With text: true, where in the text to start reading. Leave it out for the beginning; pass the text_next the previous answer gave you for the next page.

operations.summary: Put one of the client's files on the site, so a page can use it.
operations.description:
Copies the item's bytes into the site's own files and marks the catalogue item as placed. What comes back includes the `src` handle — write that into a picture element and the picture is on the page.

**Write alt text yourself, from the description.** The description lives on the catalogue item and says what the picture shows; what a picture means on a particular page is yours to say, and two pages using one image may need to describe it differently. Read the item, then write the alt onto the element that places it.

**This does not publish anything.** The bytes go into the site your client is working on, not the site the public sees. Publishing stays their decision, exactly as it is for every other change you make.

**Some material cannot be placed, and the refusal is the point.** Anything we fetched from somebody else's website is not ours to republish under your client's name, and asking again will not change the answer. Use it as reference and ask the client for something of their own.

If the name is already taken on the site by something else it is renamed rather than overwritten, so placing never replaces a different picture that is live. What came back tells you the name it actually got.

**Several framings of one picture.** To use one upload cropped several ways — a montage, a contact sheet — place it once per framing, each with its own `as` name, then crop each placed file by its site name with `edit_image`. Each file's crop is its own; a crop made on the Library item reaches only the placed files that have none of their own.

as.description: The filename to store it under on the site. Defaults to the client's own filename, which is usually what you want. A name that is not already one of this item's files on the site makes a NEW file beside the ones already there, so one item can be on a site several times — each copy can then be cropped on its own with `edit_image`, under its site name. Naming one of the item's existing files replaces that file.

operations.summary: Draw an image yourself — a mark, an icon, a divider — and keep it in the client's Library.
operations.description:
For a drawing you compose rather than a picture someone took. It is written as SVG and stored as a new item in your client's Library, with its own number (IMAGE-n) and the description you give it — exactly like a picture you generated. It is NOT on the site yet: placing it there is a separate step, the same one every Library picture takes, and it is also how a builder gets it — place it, then brief the builder with the `src` handle that placing hands back.

**Draw only what drawing is good for.** A logo starts as a WORDMARK: the business name well set — typeface, weight, spacing, maybe one simple rule or mark — which the page's own typography does better than any drawing and keeps crisp and editable. An ILLUSTRATED mark comes from image generation, iterated with your client, not from paths you plot by hand. Draw by hand for simple geometric marks, icons and dividers.

**Look before you use it.** After drawing, `screenshot` it by the `item` that comes back — that is you looking at it, not reading about it. Once it is placed, look at the page where it sits, at its real size, before you call it done or brief anything around it.

**It is drawing only, and the rules are checked rather than trusted.** Shapes, paths, gradients, text and grouping. No script, no event handler, no stylesheet, no reference to anything outside the drawing itself, and nothing that loads or embeds another document. Any of those and the whole drawing is refused, nothing is stored, and the refusal says which one. This is not a formality: once placed, the drawing is served from the site's own address, so anything executable in it would run as the site.

**Never draw a stand-in for a file the client gave you.** If they sent a logo, a photograph or a mark and you cannot find it or cannot use it, SAY SO and ask them to drop it on the conversation — do not compose something similar. A drawing offered in place of their own file is a different thing wearing its name.

**Show them what you drew.** The result carries a `display` line — paste it into your reply, word for word, where the picture belongs in what you are saying. Where it is absent there is nowhere to show it, and saying what you drew is all you can do.

**Say what it shows on the element that places it.** The `description` you give is kept with the Library item; the picture element that puts the drawing on a page has its own field for what someone who cannot see it needs told, and that is where it goes.

**A run of styled text is ONE `<text>` with `<tspan>` children — never several `<text>` elements placed by hand.** The browser advances the pen from one run to the next; positioning runs separately means guessing at gaps that are wrong on every machine but one. **Name a real font** — `system-ui`, `-apple-system` and a bare `sans-serif` resolve to different faces per platform. **Give a node an `id`** when you mean to position it precisely: once the drawing is on the site, `measure_drawing`, `relate` and `solve` address it that way.

**A redraw is a new item.** Drawing again makes another IMAGE-n; place the one you settle on. This is not a way to make a photograph.

svg.description: The drawing itself, as a complete `<svg>` document.

description.description: What the drawing shows, in the words someone would search the Library by — and what the alt text on the page will be written from.

operations.summary: Change what one of your client's uploads is for: on the site, or background reading. Only when they ask.
operations.description:
A file's role says what your client wants it used for. `site` means they want it on the site, and only then can it be placed; `reference` means it is background for you to read.

**The role is your client's decision, not yours.** Change it when they ask — "use those photos on the site" — or ask them first and change it when they say yes. Never change it because you would like to use a file. After you change it, tell them in the conversation that you did.

Only files your client uploaded themselves can be changed. A file already on the site cannot go back to `reference`. Setting `site` does not place anything; placing it is a separate step.

role.description: `site` to make it usable on the site, `reference` for background reading.

operations.summary: Delete an item from your client's Library. Only when they tell you to, in this conversation.
operations.description:
Removes the item from the Library: the file, what was written about it, and any edits made to it. It is the same thing your client's own Delete button does.

**Only on your client's instruction, given in this conversation.** Never delete on your own judgement — not to tidy duplicates, not because a picture is poor. You may suggest deleting something; they decide.

**It does not take anything off the site.** A picture already placed stays on its page, because the site keeps its own copy. The result says so; tell your client. To take it off the page as well, edit the page.

There is no undo. To have it back, your client uploads it again.

groups.title: Looking at the client's Library
groups.description: What the client has given you and what you have made for them, and what each item is. Nothing here changes anything — reading the catalogue does not put anything on the site.

groups.title: Putting the client's files on the site
groups.description: Taking something out of the client's Library and putting it on their site. Its own capability, and deliberately separate from looking: the Library is the client's private material and the site is what they publish, so this is a copy across that line and a decision rather than a lookup.

groups.title: Drawing images
groups.description: Composing an image yourself and keeping it in the client's Library. Its own capability: every other picture in the Library was chosen by a person or generated from a prompt they saw, and this is the one composed by hand. It is the consultant's — a builder places what the consultant drew and never draws.

groups.title: Keeping the client's Library, on their say-so
groups.description: Changing what an upload is for, and deleting an item — the two corrections your client can make on their own Library tab, made for them when they ask. Neither is yours to decide.

sequences.name: Choosing a picture for a page
sequences.note: Look at the candidates before you choose — screenshot takes the catalogue name unchanged, so a name from the listing needs no translating. Read the one you chose for its description, place it, and write the src handle you get back into a picture element, with alt text you wrote yourself from that description.

sequences.name: Draw a mark and use it
sequences.note: Draw, then look at it with screenshot before anything else. Place the one you settle on, and put the src handle you get back into a picture element — or brief a builder with it. Look at the page it sits on once it is there.

absences.name: Changing an item's rights
absences.note: There is no way to change an item's rights or whether it may be published, except through what it is for, and only for files your client uploaded. Rights are settled by where a file came from, and anything fetched from elsewhere stays reference whatever anyone wants.

absences.name: Taking something off the site
absences.note: Nothing here takes a picture off a page. Deleting a Library item leaves the site's copy where it is. To stop showing a picture, edit the page that shows it.

absences.name: Putting a picture in front of anybody
absences.note: Placing is not page editing. It puts the bytes on the site and hands you the handle; the picture appears to a visitor only once you write that handle into an element on a page.

absences.name: Showing a picture any way but pasting the line
absences.note: You cannot put a picture in front of your user directly — nothing you return is shown to them. What they read is your own reply and nothing else, so a picture reaches them only by the `display` line travelling into it unchanged. A turn that made a drawing and did not paste its line is a turn that left the picture where only you can see it, and the client is left to go and find it for themselves. When a result carries one, use it.
